h: 1,600 'foreigners', and 13 crore names struck off
dek: Bloomberg columnist Andy Mukherjee says the noise about infiltration is far louder than the evidence, and an odd alliance of 'cockroach' youth and the Congress could jam the Modi machine.
body: That Andy Mukherjee, who writes about markets, is writing about this movement is itself a signal. He says the Gen Z protest that began against corruption in higher education has now become a major challenge for the Modi government, and at its centre is the question of 13 crore voters left off the draft rolls. He places it alongside youth movements against entrenched elites in Paris, Madrid and Belgrade.

In Mukherjee's view the movement has moved with care. The education minister's exit was the sacrifice of just one minister, but if the election process itself looks tainted, Modi's mandate weakens. That is why the young protesters turned their aim to the ballot box.

The sharpest part of the piece deals with the infiltration argument. Amit Shah presents the drive as 'detect, delete, deport', but the writer cites a Hindustan Times investigation across six states that found only 1,600 suspected foreigners among nearly 10 crore voters. He compares this with Trump's claims, made without evidence, about non-citizens voting in America. In Bengal, women and Muslims were cut out of proportion to their numbers, and 33 percent of voters were missing from Delhi's draft roll.

Delhi Police detained and beat students, and the writer says this shocked even urban Hindu middle-class parents who usually vote for the BJP. In elections to graduate and teacher seats, the ruling alliance lost in Varanasi and Nagpur.

Mukherjee sees the next test in Uttar Pradesh, and reads the plans for delimitation and simultaneous elections as moves that shift power to the north. He says Modi, who has broken Nehru's record, holds his capital only as long as people trust elections. Censorship and detentions may wear the movement down, yet he finds it ironic that an old dynasty and young people who call themselves 'cockroaches' could together jam that machine.
nazar: The ratio of 1,600 to 10 crore mirrors this entire debate. The figures from Bengal and Delhi show who paid the price for a purge sold as protection against infiltration. When a columnist who watches markets from outside says trust is Modi's real capital, it stings the government more than any opposition speech.
sawal: If 1,600 suspects turned up among 10 crore, why were the other names cut?
ref: Gen Z
Roughly the generation born between 1997 and 2012; the writer says India has about 40 crore of them.
Delimitation
Redrawing of Lok Sabha seats based on the census, which could add seats for the populous northern states.
ank: suspected foreigners found in six states
voters left off the draft rolls

h: Bengal's deleted names, and the sinking credibility of the Election Commission
dek: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor tells readers around the world why India's Election Commission, once a model, now faces charges of bias, opacity and mass disenfranchisement, and why Gyanesh Kumar cannot hold on to his chair.
body: Shashi Tharoor tells the story from the start for readers abroad. The youth movement that rose against the education system in the summer cost Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan his job. Tharoor says that victory emboldened the protesters, who have now reached the machinery of elections. The Election Commission, once respected at home and abroad, today faces charges of bias, opacity and taking away people's right to vote.

Bengal is at the heart of his argument. In the five states that voted in April, the Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls, or SIR, removed 91 lakh names from Bengal alone. Tharoor says this went far beyond the usual pruning for deaths and migration. An automated system flagged people as 'logical discrepancies' over trivial mismatches such as the spelling of a name, checks were lax, and the people hit hardest were marginalised communities, migrant workers from villages and the urban working poor.

The numbers are his sharpest evidence. About 34 lakh people appealed, the Commission heard only around 82,000 before the election, and 91 percent of those were found valid. Tharoor concludes that most names were wrongly deleted and were not restored before the vote. The BJP won Bengal for the first time, taking 207 of 294 seats. He accepts that deletions alone did not decide the result, but says this is where the anger began.

Then more layers came to light: illegal changes to Form 6, a flood of bulk objections through Form 7, and centrally run software that allegedly stopped local officials from correcting errors. The writer says more than 13 crore names were deleted across the country. The Commission at first refused to release detailed data, and two commissioners recorded written objections to Gyanesh Kumar's unilateral decisions.

In September and October there were sit-ins and marches to the Supreme Court and the Commission; despite police water cannon and detentions, the movement stayed peaceful. Tharoor complains that the court did not give the irregularities full attention. The Commission has stopped arbitrary deletions in the remaining states and is letting names stay on the roll until appeals are decided, but calls it all 'routine'. Tharoor expects concessions, but says the crisis will not settle without Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
nazar: It is worth remembering that Tharoor is himself a Congress MP. But the strength of his piece is not in slogans; it is in one simple sum: of the appeals that were heard, nine in ten turned out to be valid. If the Commission's own hearings say this, who were the people behind the lakhs of appeals that never got a hearing? Mostly the ones whose papers are always shaky: migrant workers, poor women, minorities.

This piece is travelling to newspapers around the world through Project Syndicate. That means the question of 'vote theft' is no longer a domestic political quarrel; the credibility of India's democracy will be judged abroad on this same scale.
sawal: If nine in ten appeals were valid, what about the lakhs that were never heard?
ref: Logical discrepancy
A label used by the SIR software that put a voter under suspicion over small differences such as the spelling of a name or age.
Project Syndicate
A Prague-based organisation that places articles by leaders and scholars in hundreds of newspapers worldwide at the same time.

h: Whom is the ruling party saving democracy from?
dek: Manish Kumar of The Federal asks why the BJP, which rules the Centre and 21 states, is marching to 'save democracy' when it should have answered the questions about SIR with data.
body: Manish Kumar's explainer opens with a clash of two slogans. The opposition says 'Save the vote, save the country'; the BJP replies 'Save democracy, drive out anarchy'. The writer's question is simple: a party that has held the Centre for twelve years, and that rules, alone or with allies, 21 states and union territories covering about 72 percent of the country, is saving democracy from whom?

On one side was the rally at Ramlila Maidan; on the other, the BJP's padyatras (foot marches) and road shows: Amit Shah with the tricolour in Hyderabad, JP Nadda in Bareilly, party president Nitin Nabin in Kolkata and Gorakhpur. The opposition is angry that SIR removed about 13 crore names, roughly 15 percent of voters, from the rolls, and alleges people were cut by branding them infiltrators, with minorities and women hit hardest.

The writer also records reports from inside the Commission. According to the Indian Express, Gyanesh Kumar ran the Commission arbitrarily, and commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi raised written objections fourteen times in ten months, on matters from SIR to the changes in Form 6. The Commission has quietly reversed some decisions, but neither the Chief Election Commissioner nor the two commissioners have spoken.

The BJP argues that SIR was needed to remove fake, duplicate and ineligible names, and that the opposition is defaming constitutional bodies. The party also claimed that rallies during the festival season cost traders Rs 10,000 to 15,000 crore. The writer reminds readers that protecting the credibility of institutions, clean elections and room for dissent is the government's own duty.

Citing critics, he lists three reasons: political counter-attack, fear that the 'vote theft' charge is reaching ordinary voters, and worry about the 2027 assembly and 2029 Lok Sabha elections. His conclusion is that marches will not make the SIR questions go away; they must be answered with facts, not on the streets.
nazar: When a government starts taking out protest marches itself, it is admitting that the debate is slipping out of its hands. The writer's most precise question is why the head of the Commission that ministers are defending on the streets is himself silent. Those whose names were cut need booth-level accounts, not slogans.
sawal: Whom is a party that rules 21 states saving democracy from?
ref: Form 6
The statutory form for adding a new name to the electoral roll; the Commission is accused of adding an extra declaration to it without Parliament's approval.

h: Shielding Gyanesh Kumar is now a test of the government's own credibility
dek: On Navbharat's editorial page, Narendra Sharma says turning the defence of the Chief Election Commissioner into a matter of prestige would be the government's biggest mistake.
body: In Navbharat's 'Vishesh' (special) editorial column, Narendra Sharma argues that the campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar is no longer just a matter of political attacks by the Congress or Rahul Gandhi. In his view the question is now about an institution's credibility, built from the Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls, or SIR, complaints of deleted names, and charges of unilateral decisions inside the Commission.

The writer sees as the turning point the September report that two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, recorded written objections at least fourteen times in ten months. In his view this gave the opposition ground to say the matter was not just a tussle between government and opposition, but about how the Commission makes decisions. The symbolic 'people's impeachment' by nineteen parties, and then the Ramlila Maidan rally, stood on this ground.

The most interesting part of the editorial is about the government's dilemma. The writer says the harder the government defends Gyanesh Kumar, the more people ask why it is so invested in this officer. On the other hand, if he is made to resign, Rahul Gandhi will call it his victory. And the Chief Election Commissioner is no ordinary officer to be removed at will; under Article 324(5), that needs a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.

Sharma also notes Rahul Gandhi's point that the vote is the common man's greatest political power, and that doubt over the electoral roll hollows out the whole election process. In his view a common perception is taking hold that the Commission is under the government's influence and that the opposition's complaints are not heard seriously.

In conclusion the writer advises the government not to make the defence of Gyanesh Kumar a question of prestige, but to focus on restoring trust in the Commission. In his view the institution on which every election rests is bigger than any one person's chair.
nazar: This editorial matters because it comes not from an opposition paper but from a mainstream Hindi daily that usually avoids confronting the government. When even such a paper says the Commission's credibility is at stake, it is clear that the 'vote theft' question has stepped off the rally stage and become an ordinary reader's worry.

But the advice to restore credibility is incomplete if it says nothing of the people whose names were cut from the roll. An institution's trust returns not through a press release, but when the name of the last voter who had no papers is put back.
sawal: Hard to remove the officer, costly to protect him: what will the government choose?
ref: Article 324(5)
The constitutional provision under which the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge, that is, by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
People's impeachment
A symbolic event on 30 October by nineteen parties of the INDIA alliance, in which the Chief Election Commissioner was 'tried' in the style of a people's court.

h: A debate challenge was fine in 2013, so why is it 'drama' now?
dek: Siasat's editorial says that since the Ramlila rally, Amit Shah, not the Prime Minister, has been answering Rahul Gandhi's questions, and that this silence is what is sharpening the confrontation.
body: In its 6 November editorial, the Hyderabad Urdu daily Siasat calls the mood after the 1 November Delhi rally a 'political confrontation'. The paper says that since this INDIA alliance gathering, political activity has picked up across the country, remarks on both sides have grown sharper, and each side is busy taking its case straight to the people.

In the editorial's view, the change is that Rahul Gandhi is now aiming directly at Prime Minister Narendra Modi rather than at ministers or officials. He is asking questions, challenging him to an open debate, and also alleging that Modi came to power with outside help and stays there with its support. The Prime Minister is silent; Home Minister Amit Shah is answering, saying the debate should happen in Parliament and that Rahul Gandhi is doing 'drama politics' on the streets.

The paper reminds readers that the Prime Minister himself started this war of words, when in a speech he mocked the Congress for launching a 'failed product' again and again. The editorial accuses the BJP of double standards: in 2013, as Gujarat chief minister and prime ministerial candidate, Modi himself challenged then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to a debate on the economy, and nobody pointed to Parliament then.

The editorial also takes a jab at Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta's challenge to Rahul Gandhi to debate in Parliament, when she herself is not a member of Parliament. The paper says the Prime Minister should answer national questions, and that his silence is what is spreading the confrontation across the country.

Finally Siasat writes that the government has launched a big campaign against Rahul Gandhi because it feels he is drawing attention by raising people's issues. The paper says the questions being asked are on people's minds too, and sooner or later the government will have to answer them.
nazar: The real demand of the Ramlila rally, accountability for the voter rolls and the Commission, has fallen behind in this editorial, and the debate has settled into a war of words between Rahul and Shah. That is the danger: when a movement turns into sparring between leaders, the lakhs of people whose names were cut drop out of the news.
Still, Siasat has a point that the question should be answered by the person it was asked of. In a democracy the Prime Minister's silence is also a statement, and that statement reaches the people.
sawal: How did a debate challenge to Manmohan Singh become 'drama' now?
ref: Siasat
An Urdu daily published from Hyderabad since 1949, one of the oldest and largest Urdu newspapers in South India.
Ramlila rally
The INDIA alliance's 'Save the vote, save the country' rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on 1 November 2026, where the demand for the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation was raised.

h: After Ramlila, what next: a boycott, or a satyagraha like the salt march?
dek: Hyderabad columnist Sarfaraz Ahmed Qasmi asks which way the rally's energy will now go, and answers by recalling the Dandi March.
body: Senior Hyderabad journalist and columnist Sarfaraz Ahmed Qasmi takes stock of the 1 November rally on the Urdu portal Al-Hilal Media. He begins by recording the claims made from the stage: Rahul Gandhi saying Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar will be removed and go to jail, and that the 2024 election was illegitimate; Mallikarjun Kharge's charge that the names of Dalits, women and Adivasis (indigenous communities) were deleted; Akhilesh Yadav's claim that 1.27 crore voters were removed in Uttar Pradesh. These are all allegations.

Qasmi says the country's politics is now split into two camps, and the 2027 elections in five states including Uttar Pradesh will set the country's direction, so for the opposition this is a fight for survival. He believes Nitish Kumar and Chandrababu Naidu moving to the NDA and Mamata Banerjee's defeat in Bengal had weakened the alliance, but Ramlila has unsettled the ruling side.

The writer also traces the movement's roots: the revision of voter rolls that began in Bihar in June, then the 'Cockroach Party' and student groups joining in. He says observers see the Jantar Mantar protest as the real engine of the campaign. Now the demands have grown: scrap SIR, prosecute Gyanesh Kumar, and repeal the 2023 law that changed how commissioners are appointed.

But Qasmi says the parliament of the streets and the 'people's impeachment' will matter only if the opposition secures corrected voter rolls and wins the coming state elections. Behind the BJP's confidence he sees unease, and recalls Gujarat in 2018, when the slogan of '150 plus' got stuck below a hundred.

The article's real question comes at the end: what should the next step be? An appeal not to vote, a boycott of state elections or of Parliament, or civil disobedience? Here the writer recalls the 1930 Dandi March, which began at Sabarmati with 78 companions, went on to break the salt law, and spread across the country. He says that movement was bigger than salt; this one too can be bigger than the vote, but the road is not yet decided.
nazar: Of the options Qasmi lists, a boycott is the most dangerous. For people whose names have already been cut from the rolls, an appeal not to vote would be a second eviction. The Dandi example is useful because it was not a movement of staying away from something, but of openly breaking an unjust law and bringing ordinary people into it.

Today's salt may be Form 6: going village to village to get every deleted name added back. It is less glamorous than a rally, but in Uttar Pradesh's next election it will decide whether the Ramlila crowd reached the booth or not.
sawal: In the fight for the vote, what will today's salt be?
ref: Dandi March
Gandhi's 1930 march of about 390 kilometres from Sabarmati to Dandi, in which the British salt law was broken and the civil disobedience movement began.
2023 appointments law

The law on appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and commissioners, which removed the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee and added a Union minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

h: The test of Ramlila's unity: the BSP and AAP
dek: Ajit Dwivedi says the twenty-party platform will be tested in next year's elections in seven states, where the biggest obstacle is the BSP and the Aam Aadmi Party standing outside the alliance.
body: In his column 'Nabz Par Haath' (finger on the pulse), senior journalist Ajit Dwivedi treats the Ramlila Maidan rally as only a beginning. Leaders of twenty parties were on stage, but the Bahujan Samaj Party and the Aam Aadmi Party were not, and the writer says these two will decide whether this unity turns into votes. The first test will come in February in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Punjab, Goa and Manipur, then at the end of the year in Himachal and Gujarat.

The writer recalls that after the 2024 setback the BJP bounced back by winning Maharashtra, Haryana, Delhi, Bihar, West Bengal and Assam. In these seven states too it is the main contender, and it governs five of them. Except in Uttar Pradesh, the Congress is in a direct contest in the other six, and Dwivedi says the other opposition parties will accept Congress leadership only if it shows it can win on its own.

The writer's longest argument is about Uttar Pradesh. The fight there is three-cornered; the BSP still has about ten percent of the vote, and more than half of the state's roughly twenty percent Dalit voters are Jatavs, who he says are still emotionally tied to Mayawati. Chandrashekhar Azad's party and the Congress are trying to break into this vote, but it is not easy. The SP and the Congress together won 43 Lok Sabha seats in 2024; the writer says the BSP's Brahmin and Muslim candidates are the biggest hurdle to repeating that result.

In Punjab and Goa, the Aam Aadmi Party and the Congress will face each other. In Gujarat last time AAP took about thirteen percent of the vote, mostly from the Congress, and in Goa AAP and the Trinamool together took about the same. In Punjab the BJP won no seat in 2024 but still took eighteen percent of the vote, and now wants the role of big brother with the Akali Dal.
Uttarakhand and Himachal are straight fights. In the writer's view, only if the Congress wins some of these states on its own strength will its standing inside the alliance rise.
nazar: Dwivedi's arithmetic is cold, but necessary. The Ramlila crowd made the right to vote an issue, but in the states where the next test comes, the opposition vote is itself divided. A movement whose slogan is 'save the vote' also faces the question of keeping the votes that remain from cutting into each other.

One gap is that the piece leaves the names deleted in SIR out of this sum. If lakhs of Dalits, Muslims and migrant workers in Uttar Pradesh stayed off the rolls, every estimate of a three-cornered fight could change.
sawal: If the Jatav vote stays with Mayawati, how much will Ramlila's unity help?
ref: Nabz Par Haath
Ajit Dwivedi's regular political column in Naya India.
Jatav
The largest Dalit community in Uttar Pradesh, long the core base of the BSP.

h: Six years, seven bail pleas, and a medium pacer in jail
dek: Aseem Sundan has written an open letter to his friend Umar Khalid, saying the new generation has begun to see past the 'face' the government built.
body: On 13 September Umar Khalid completed six years in jail, without his trial being completed. His friend Aseem Sundan has written him an open letter on Maktoob Media. He says every bail hearing is like the punishment of Sisyphus: the stone reaches the top and the court rolls it back down. Seven pleas have been rejected.

The most personal part of the letter is a conversation about cricket. During his last bail, watching kites fly over a rooftop, Umar said he considers himself a decent medium pacer and waits every year for the Tihar cricket tournament. The writer argues that such small things are what make someone human, and that this is what power wants to take from Umar, while even friends reduce him to a mere symbol of courage.

Sundan claims the labels 'terrorist' and 'anti-national' are losing their force. At recent youth protests, when right-wing channels asked about him, most young people spoke of a fair trial. Gen Z was very young in the era of that old propaganda, so it sees Umar as a researcher, whose book on Adivasi (indigenous) history, 'Fractured Communities', is being read.

The writer says memes inciting violence against Umar were posted on the BJP's state-level pages, while the 'Free Umar Khalid' Instagram page was blocked in India under the IT law. In Goa in August, an FIR was filed against a student holding a placard for his release. The writer alleges that his Muslim name has made Umar a political untouchable, so fewer questions are raised about the injustice done to him.

Finally Sundan mentions an essay by Pema, a Class 8 student in a remote village in Himachal, titled 'My Inspiration', on Umar Khalid. For the writer this is proof that jail has held back the man, not his ideas.
nazar: Six years in prison under the UAPA without a trial is a punishment in itself, whatever the verdict. In our view this letter matters because it turns Umar Khalid from a slogan back into a human being, and reminds us that the principle 'bail is the rule, jail the exception' has been turned upside down for Muslim and dissenting voices.
sawal: Why does a researcher bowling in Tihar frighten the government?
ref: Umar Khalid

A student activist with a PhD from JNU, in jail since September 2020 under the UAPA in the case of an alleged 'conspiracy' behind the 2020 Delhi riots.
The trial is not yet complete, and several courts have refused him bail.
Sisyphus

A figure from Greek myth, punished to push a stone up a mountain only for it to roll back down every time.
A symbol of pointless, endless toil.

h: Extreme weather is now an everyday thing: 16,000 deaths in five years
dek: An assessment by Down To Earth and CSE finds that between 2022 and 2026 the weather struck somewhere in India on almost every day of the year, with the worst damage in the last three years.
body: Richard Mahapatra and Kiran Pandey present the gist of the latest assessment by the Centre for Science and Environment, and its core finding is that in India 'a disaster every day' has become normal. Looking at January to September, in 2022 and 2023 there was lightning, a flood, a heatwave or a landslide somewhere on 86 to 88 percent of days. In 2025 this figure reached 99 percent, and in 2026, 251 of 273 days were like this.

The death toll stings even more. About 16,200 people died in five years, nearly two-thirds of them after 2024. In 2025 the number was 4,064, the highest in five years. Farming took a hit on at least 2 crore hectares of crops, and in 2025 alone about 95 lakh hectares were destroyed.

The hardest-hit states include Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Assam. In Madhya Pradesh, 748 of 1,366 days saw some extreme event. In the east and northeast, the share of such days rose from 63 to 80 percent.

The report also points to shifting seasons. Winters are getting warmer, not a single cold wave day was recorded in February 2026, and in Himachal a heatwave set in at the start of March, 74 days earlier than in 2024. In just the three months before the monsoon, more than 7 lakh hectares of crops were lost, which means the season of danger for farmers is no longer only the rains.
The writers conclude that no part of the country has been spared. Events vary by region and season, but overall the risk is rising everywhere: not ups and downs, but a steady climb.
nazar: These figures are not just a climate debate; they are an account of poor people's livelihoods. For farm workers in the heat, herders killed by lightning, mud houses sinking in floods, 'disaster' is no longer an occasional event. In our view, when there is a disaster every day, relief must also go beyond one-time compensation, to crop insurance, work rules for labourers during heatwaves, and a firm system of village-level warnings.
sawal: What did a February without a cold wave write on the ears of wheat?
ref: CSE

Centre for Science and Environment, a Delhi research and advocacy body that publishes Down To Earth magazine.
Every year it releases an assessment of extreme weather events called 'Climate India'.

h: Pakistan's journalists write the news, but pizza pays the bills
dek: In The Friday Times, Naeem Ahmed writes that salaries held back for years, or paid only in part, in the small towns of Punjab are hollowing out journalism from within.
body: A journalist who has worked for Geo News in Faisalabad for fifteen years has not had a raise in all that time, so he sells clothes online to run his home. A Dunya News reporter has opened a pizza shop. A crime reporter at the Jang newspaper with twenty years behind him says he does not get even half the minimum wage set by the Punjab government, and even that comes months late. Naeem Ahmed begins his investigation with these people.

There is no official data on journalists' pay, but the president of the Faisalabad Union of Journalists estimates that 90 percent of the more than five thousand registered newspapers in Punjab do not pay salaries every month at all. Women are worse off: they are paid less, and their work is seen as a hobby, not a profession.

A legal framework exists on paper. Under a 1973 law, a wage board sets pay scales for newspaper employees, but the eighth award came sixteen years late. TV, radio and digital media are outside its scope. Owners point to falling circulation, costly newsprint and government advertising rates that have not risen in years. In September a National Assembly committee said the burden of government dues cannot be passed on to workers, and asked for details of payments.

The writer sought information from several departments under the right to information, but got no reply, so he had to file appeals. He suggests that government advertising should go only to outlets that pay salaries on time and give written contracts.

His main argument is that this is not an internal quarrel between owner and employee, but a public matter. A hard-up reporter bends more quickly under pressure, experienced people leave the profession, and news from small towns stops being published. Free journalism needs not only freedom from censorship but also a guarantee of a full stomach.
nazar: This picture is not unfamiliar on this side of the border either. Stringers in India's districts and small towns work without contracts for small sums paid per story, and since the Working Journalists Act was merged into the new labour codes, their protection has grown weaker. In our view, the fight for press freedom is also fought over the pay slip.
sawal: Whom can a reporter whose salary is months overdue stand up to?
ref: Wage board (Pakistan)

A board set up under the 1973 Newspaper Employees law that fixes pay scales and allowances for newspaper staff.
Its eighth award came sixteen years late.

h: Democrats have won Congress, but Trump has two more years
dek: Josh Paul says the real power of the Democrats' big win lies in the budget and investigating committees, but the party's own old structure may be the biggest obstacle to a progressive agenda.
body: In the US midterm elections the Democratic Party has taken both the House and the Senate. Josh Paul calls it a historic win, but reminds readers that Donald Trump will stay in the White House for two more years. So he says the new Congress has three paths: reining in Trump, preparing its own agenda for 2028, and working with the administration on a few issues such as AI.

The list of checks is long: stopping the Iran war, blocking judicial appointments, ending ICE's indiscriminate detentions, and investigating the money networks of Trump and those close to him. But the writer says plainly that most bills will be stopped by the presidential veto, and the administration will ignore measures such as war powers resolutions. Still, votes on issues like sending arms to Israel matter, because they set the direction of debate and put every member on record.

The real weapon is the budget. If Republicans fail to pass a budget before the year ends, Democrats will decide spending for the next two years. That includes the $3.3 billion in annual aid to Israel, which Trump himself questioned on election day. The ban on UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, could also be reopened.

But the writer's sharpest point is about the party itself. Committee chairs go by seniority, and senior leaders shy away from questioning ties with Israel. The party's base wants hearings on America's role in Gaza, but such hearings would also put senior officials of the Biden administration in the dock.

Paul's conclusion is that responsibility for decisions now lies with the Democrats. Debates that were put off while in opposition, especially on Israel, can no longer be put off. If the party cannot offer credible leadership for change, the 'America First' right could leave it behind.
nazar: This win is welcome news for the world, but Paul's warning applies to every democracy: winning an election and changing the structure of power are two different tasks. In India too, after every opposition win, the same question comes up of how much room old leaders will give to new demands.
The demand for hearings on Gaza is a mirror for America. How will a party that avoids holding its own officials to account win the trust of people on the margins of the world?
sawal: Will chairs won by seniority allow a hearing on Gaza?
ref: Josh Paul
A former US State Department official who resigned in October 2023 in protest against arms shipments to Israel.
Power of the purse
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to approve government spending, so the budget is its biggest lever.

h: American voters demanded an accounting for the Iran war and Gaza
dek: Jason Jones argues that the midterms were decided not only by inflation but also by anger over Gaza and the Iran war, and that this feeling belongs to no single party.
body: Human rights activist Jason Jones believes that calling this year's US midterm election only a story about inflation is incomplete. He says public anger over Gaza and the Iran war played a big part in the Democrats' win, and the clearest example is Michigan.

There, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers for a Senate seat. The writer says that in the Democratic primary the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC and groups linked to it poured about $30 million into backing Haley Stevens, their biggest spending on a single seat so far. Even after the primary was lost, money kept flowing against El-Sayed, and a few days before the election Stevens herself endorsed the Republican candidate, because El-Sayed questioned Israel's military action and the American money behind it.

What is interesting is that this is now coming from inside the ruling side too. The writer says that the day after the results, Vice President JD Vance listed four voter concerns, including ending the Iran war and changing ties with Israel. In an election night survey published by Responsible Statecraft, 62 percent of voters called the Iran war a mistake and 74 percent said it had a big effect on their vote.

Jones argues that the coalition that elected Trump in 2024 stood on opposition to 'endless wars', and that the Iran war breaks faith with those voters. People also linked rising kitchen costs to this war and to aid for Israel. He also names settler violence in the West Bank, including attacks on old Christian communities, as a 2028 danger for Republicans.
The article's final point is that anti-war feeling is not the property of the Democrats but of ordinary Americans. Leaders who ignore it could be replaced by voters.
nazar: A lobby's money losing in America is no small thing. In India too elections are often fought over kitchen costs, but this piece shows that voters understand the link between a distant war and their own pockets, provided someone tells them the truth.

Still, caution is needed: drawing the meaning of a whole election from one survey and one seat is the writer's own reading. The real test will be what the new Congress does about arms shipments for Gaza.
sawal: What did Michigan teach the lobby by defeating its $30 million?
ref: AIPAC
American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, which spends heavily in elections.
Responsible Statecraft
The online publication of the Quincy Institute, which argues for a restrained foreign policy against US military intervention.

h: The blue wave did not fall from the sky; people built it
dek: Social psychologist Emese Ilyés says the midterm results are a victory not for leaders but for organised people, and that the party should follow the movements.
body: Emese Ilyés researches community resistance and ways of living together in times of authoritarianism. The day after the election she asks what this feeling is: relief, joy, or the surprise that despite money and power, ordinary people's voices could not be silenced.

She lists the many firsts in the results: several Black governors at once for the first time, the first Native woman governor, the first Muslim senator, and the first Latina governor, who defeated Greg Abbott in Texas. Former schoolteacher James Talarico, who reached the Senate from Texas, took no corporate money. The writer says Elon Musk alone gave $474 million in this election, of which $168 million went just into trying to defeat Talarico.

Ilyés stresses that the story should not be woven around any one name. Behind every win were thousands of people who knocked on doors, refused, and looked after one another. Early voting was 90 lakh (9 million) higher than in 2022.

Here she turns to psychology. In Martin Seligman's famous experiment, dogs that were shocked again and again stopped moving even when a way out opened, which was called 'learned helplessness'. Later Seligman himself accepted that what is actually learned is a sense of one's own power, and that it is built together. Ignacio Martín-Baró, the Salvadoran priest and psychologist, also said that faith in fate is nothing natural; systems produce it.
The writer also remembers neighbours being deported without a hearing, and universities whose freedom is being taken away. For her the vote is one task among many, and hope is a practice.
nazar: Here too, after every election the win is written in the name of a single face. Ilyés's point is just as true for India: the nameless workers standing at the booth and the neighbourhood networks are the answer to helplessness.
The defeat of the huge spending of one man like Musk also shows that transparency in election funding is a basic need of every democracy.
sawal: When does a dog being shocked see the open way out?
ref: Learned helplessness
Psychologist Martin Seligman's theory that after repeated failure a creature stops trying.
Ignacio Martín-Baró
A Jesuit priest from El Salvador and one of the founders of 'liberation psychology'; he was killed on 16 November 1989 by a US-trained army unit.

h: The 24 hours start at detention, not at the arrest paperwork
dek: The Supreme Court said the deadline for producing a person before a magistrate runs from the moment police take away their liberty, and ordered the release of four people held unaccounted for 18 hours.
body: On 5 November the Supreme Court made it clear that the 24-hour deadline for producing a person before a magistrate begins the moment the police stop them, not when an arrest is recorded on paper. A bench of Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S. Chandurkar gave the ruling in Sujit Das v. Union of India.

The case came from Tripura. Four people were stopped at 2 pm on 29 September 2025 during a search in which 11.03 kg of yaba tablets were allegedly recovered. But the record showed their arrest at 11 am the next day. That means they were in police custody for about 18 hours with no court watching over them. The Tripura High Court had refused them bail.

According to the bench, drawing a line between 'arrest' and 'detention' for the purpose of Article 22(2) does not stand the test of the Constitution. Only the time needed to travel to the magistrate's court can be left out of the 24 hours. The court rejected rulings of the Odisha, Kerala and Madras High Courts that had taken the opposite view.

Magistrates will now have to record the real date and time of detention, and if the deadline has been crossed, the accused must be released. Even within 24 hours, if the detention seems longer than the circumstances needed, the magistrate can refuse remand under Section 58 of the BNSS. The four appellants were ordered to be freed at once.
nazar: Last month thousands of people across the country were picked up 'as a precaution'; many were driven around for hours in buses and kept in police stations, and the paperwork came later. This ruling is a tool in every such case: the clock starts the moment a hand is laid on you. The real test will be in the lower courts, where magistrates often accept the date written by the police without a question.
sawal: Who will account for the 18 hours before the arrest on paper?
ref: Article 22(2)
The constitutional rule that an arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, or the detention becomes illegal.
Section 58 of the BNSS
The rule in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita that police cannot hold a person arrested without a warrant for longer than is reasonable, and never beyond 24 hours.

h: Goa: they changed address and lost their votes; High Court pulls up the Commission
dek: The Goa bench of the Bombay High Court ordered six names of one family, cut in SIR, restored within ten days, and called the condition imposed on voters who had moved house a 'Catch-22'.
body: On 5 November the Goa bench of the Bombay High Court told the Election Commission to put the names of six members of the Salgaonkar family back on the voter roll. The names had been cut during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Goa. A bench of Justice Valmiki Menezes and Justice Amit Jamsandekar directed the BLO (booth-level officer) of the Santa Cruz assembly constituency to verify the address and add the names within ten days.

After moving house, the family had filled Form 8 to correct their address. The Commission argued that under the SIR rules a pre-filled enumeration form also had to be submitted with Form 8, and it was not, so they were told to fill Form 6 like new voters.

The court questioned this very condition. The pre-filled enumeration form makes the voter declare that they still live at the old address, which means a person who has moved would be forced to make a false declaration. Justice Menezes asked why an old voter trying to fix an address should be turned into a new applicant. The bench called the situation a 'Catch-22' and also objected to Form 8 being rejected outright instead of being kept pending until verification.

The Commission's lawyer, Ashutosh Kumbhakoni, wanted the hearing put off until the Supreme Court decides the SIR cases pending before it. The bench said this case was not about the validity of SIR at all, and refused both to adjourn the hearing and to stay its order for two weeks.
nazar: Six names is a small number, but the logic is big. This same SIR condition pushes off the roll people who change rented homes or move cities for work, and migrant workers and poor tenants are hit first. The court has spotted the trap, but not everyone whose name is cut can reach a High Court.
sawal: How did moving house become a reason to erase a voter?
ref: Form 8 and Form 6
Form 8 lets an existing voter correct their address or details; Form 6 is the application to add a new voter's name.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
The Election Commission drive in which the voter roll is made afresh and every voter has to fill an enumeration form.

h: University of Hyderabad: an email calling a student a 'Dalit untouchable', and only an apology in reply
dek: A history professor is accused of casteist abuse against a former student; the department took an apology and treated the matter as closed, and the complainant is now pressing for action.
body: Dr Vijay Ramdas Mandala, associate professor in the history department of the University of Hyderabad (UoH), is accused of calling a former student a 'Dalit untouchable idiot' in an email and describing students from Bihar and Jharkhand as 'third-rate, poverty-stricken'. The complainant, Subodh Kumar, did his MA in history here in 2017-19 and is now doing a PhD at the University of Nottingham in Britain.

According to the report, some former students were working with the professor on an edited book. One of the authors cited the fieldwork rules of British universities, and this email came in reply on 16 April 2026. Eleven days later the professor also returned Subodh's chapter and said his name should not be mentioned anywhere in future.

The first complaint went to the head of department, Prof. Y. Swarupa R. Shankar. On 10 May she wrote that the professor had given a written apology and assured that he would not interfere with any fellowship or recommendation letter, so the matter would be settled. The professor reportedly called it a 'momentary outburst of emotion'. On 13 May Subodh refused to accept this and recalled the death of Rohith Vemula.

On 31 October he sent a fresh complaint to the Vice-Chancellor, the RC Cell and the students' union, demanding disciplinary action, and has said that if no concrete step is taken he will go to the UGC, the Ministry of Education and the National Commission for Scheduled Castes. The UK unit of the SFI has demanded an open inquiry, dismissal and a case under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
nazar: Rohith Vemula was a student on this same campus, and ten years on, the answer to casteist insult here is still a letter of apology. When the department itself plays middleman and 'settles' the matter, a Dalit student is left with no reason to trust the institution. This habit of forcing compromise in place of a complaint is what keeps discrimination alive on campuses.
sawal: How was a casteist slur paid off with a letter of apology?
ref: Rohith Vemula
A Dalit research scholar at the University of Hyderabad who died by suicide in January 2016 amid suspension and discrimination.
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
A 1989 law that makes caste-based insult and harassment of Dalits and Adivasis (indigenous communities) a crime.

h: AI behind two in every five fake claims, and newsrooms fell for it too
dek: BOOM's August-October report says AI-made false content hit a record high, chatbots began calling real pictures fake, and big channels themselves became carriers of falsehood.
body: Fact-checking outlet BOOM published 165 fact-checks between 3 August and 30 October 2026, and its report released on 5 November says 65 of them, or 39.4 per cent, involved content made or altered with AI. In the first seven months of the year this share was 30.7 per cent, and in 2025 it was 20.5 per cent. September was the first month this year in which more than half the fact-checks were linked to AI.

The biggest subject was the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests against the Chief Election Commissioner, with 24 fact-checks. Half of these were old videos, such as a clip from the farmers' movement passed off as deaths at Jantar Mantar. An AI-made bail bond bearing the signature of the movement's founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and a deepfake of NSA Ajit Doval also circulated widely.

Chatbots are the new danger. Grok and Gemini called real pictures of the protests fake, and NDTV ran a fact-check video based on that answer, which it later had to take down. Mainstream media themselves carried 32 of the 165 false claims, compared with seven per cent in the previous period. News18 and ABP News came up most often.

There were 14 fact-checks on communal claims; none involved AI, but these were judged to carry the highest risk of harm. Old clips of Hindutva groups were also circulated to stir up violence against CJP supporters. Varanasi Police even called a real video AI-made and announced FIRs against people who shared it.
nazar: When an official police handle calls a real video fake and big channels treat a chatbot's answer as proof, the trade in lies is not run by trolls alone. The worst hit are those who have no other platform to show their truth: protesters, minorities and people in small towns.
sawal: If a chatbot calls a real picture fake, whose testimony do we believe?
ref: Deepfake
An AI-made video in which a real person's face or lips are altered to make them say something they never said.
Voice clone
A fake voice made by AI from samples of someone's voice, then laid over real footage.

h: Dindori: Rs 40 lakh spent, and the sal forests are still sick
dek: A drive against the sal borer in Madhya Pradesh has failed, and now a former forest chief himself is asking for a halt to the felling of one and a half lakh trees during the rains.
body: In Madhya Pradesh's Dindori district, the drive to control the sal borer, an insect eating away the sal forest, appears to have had little effect. During the monsoon the forest department spent about Rs 40 lakh and trapped nearly 20 lakh insects; 6,769 healthy trees were cut to make the traps. Yet the outbreak goes on. People in the villages of Chauradadar and Sontirath say the campaign began on time but was wound up too soon.

Last year more than 30,000 hectares of sal forest were affected. On 1 September the Centre's regional committee allowed the felling of 1,46,784 trees in Dindori and 9,535 in neighbouring Anuppur, and about a third have already been cut. But Dindori's working plan says felling should be completed before June. Because of the delay in approval, the felling happened in the rains and the cut trunks were left lying in the forest, which entomologists say can become a home for the insects.

Uday Homkar, an entomologist at the State Forest Research Institute, says the insects have already come out, nothing will be gained by more felling now, and the remaining trees should be checked again. Former Principal Chief Conservator of Forests Ram Prasad has demanded that the felling be stopped at once and asked how many trees were scientifically examined before they were marked. He cites the example of Kanha in the 1990s, where lakhs of trees were spared despite infestation.
The current forest chief, B.S. Annigeri, admitted that a second check could save some trees, and said permission to fell does not mean every marked tree must come down.
nazar: Dindori is a mostly Adivasi (indigenous) district, where sal leaves, seeds and the forest are tied to the livelihoods of many families. Here the hasty cure is proving more dangerous than the disease: the file stayed stuck in Delhi, and the axe fell in the rains. Decisions about the forest are being made without asking the people who know it best.
sawal: Who checked the green, standing trees before the axe came down?
ref: Sal borer
A beetle that bores tunnels into the trunks of sal trees; a large outbreak can dry out trees on a wide scale.
Working plan
A ten-year government plan for each forest division that decides when and how felling, protection and upkeep should be done.

h: After a post about a judge, contempt action against CJP's Ratna Singh
dek: The Delhi government has sanctioned criminal contempt against the Cockroach Janata Party's legal head, who commented on a judge after her plea for an FIR over her detention was turned down.
body: The Delhi government has sanctioned criminal contempt proceedings against Ratna Singh, head of the legal cell of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). The reason is her social media posts about a judge of the Saket district court. LiveLaw first reported the news.

On 10 October, before a CJP protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, police allegedly detained Ratna Singh and stopped her from going there. She applied for an FIR against these policemen, which the court dismissed. According to Bar and Bench, after the hearing she wrote that the judge was 'serving the master', got up several times during the proceedings, and that both the police and the judge were acting at the bidding of some unnamed 'master'.

Delhi government lawyer Amol Sinha says these remarks question the judge's independence and could weaken people's faith in the courts. In his view, criticising an order is one thing and alleging that a judge is acting on someone else's orders is another, and Ratna Singh put forward no facts to back her claim.

The sanction was given under Section 15(2) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, which allows a law officer to have criminal contempt proceedings started in the High Court. The step was taken on a lawyer's complaint.
nazar: The movement whose workers were detained on the streets now sees the woman fighting its legal battles heading for the dock. Making personal allegations against a judge is risky, but contempt law has often become a tool to frighten criticism. The government's speed shows that every case linked to the CJP is now part of a political fight.
sawal: How did the woman who asked for an FIR against the police end up in the dock herself?
ref: Criminal contempt
A statement or act that lowers the standing of a court or interferes with justice; it can carry a sentence of up to six months.
Section 15(2), Contempt of Courts Act
The High Court hears contempt of a district court only when the lower court refers it or a law officer applies.

h: The Musahar teacher who drove an auto, and the poem about a parrot
dek: Ashish Nand of Majhwa village in Mirzapur kept alive his dream of becoming a teacher through poverty, debt and auto-rickshaw fares, and is now teaching Musahar children to believe in themselves.
body: This story, published on Teachers' Day, is written by Ashish Nand himself. Twenty-five-year-old Ashish is a Musahar from Majhwa village in Uttar Pradesh's Mirzapur district. He remembers the day in Class 9 when his maths teacher, Jitendra Sharma, told him in front of the whole class to study hard and become an example for the children of his community. It was the first time Ashish saw himself that way.

Musahars are listed as a Scheduled Caste in Uttar Pradesh and for centuries have lived landless, without steady income, at the very margins. Education has rarely been part of their lives. Children left school to work, were married young, and in many homes even one meal a day was hard to arrange. In Ashish's area the community's literacy is said to be about three per cent.

His father, Pappu Banwasi, was a daily-wage labourer who ran a household of eight alone; his mother, Abha Devi, worked in the fields when she found work. Parents who had never gone to school themselves sent all five sons to study. Ashish was the first in the family to reach college, Mahatma Gandhi Kashi Vidyapith, 30 km away. In 2022 he did his BA in Hindi.

But the family's needs turned out bigger than the dream. His mother was ill, his wife was pregnant, his father earned little. As the eldest son, Ashish did labour for Rs 500 a day, then began driving a rented auto-rickshaw. He felt ashamed at first, but passing schools and talking to teachers who rode as passengers kept his dream alive.

In 2024, through his aunt, he heard of a fellowship with the organisation Muheem that involved two years of teaching Musahar children. Ashish was selected, learned to teach through play, stories and activities, and took charge of a class of 30 children. For him, a lack of confidence was a bigger enemy than poverty. One day Samar, a six- or seven-year-old who sat at the back, read out two lines about a parrot in a trembling voice, and the class clapped. The fellowship ends in September and the road ahead is not clear.
nazar: This story shows that the biggest support for children on the margins is often not a scheme but a face from among them. It also shows how thin a thread such teachers hang by: one fellowship ends and the path is uncertain again.
If governments truly want to take education to communities like the Musahars, giving young people like Ashish permanent jobs and respect should be the first step.
sawal: Who will take Samar's class when the fellowship ends?
ref: Musahar
A Dalit community of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, traditionally landless and counted as the furthest behind on every measure of education and income.

h: Gaza: telling the story, and living it too
dek: This Al Jazeera Witness film follows reporter Maram Humaid as she records the forced displacement from Gaza City while going through the same displacement herself with her family.
by: Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah Al-Haw, Ibrahim Al-Otla
body: Usually in war reporting the journalist stays behind the camera and the story belongs to someone else. This film from Al Jazeera's Witness series erases that distance. Its central figure is Maram Humaid, Al Jazeera's correspondent in Gaza, who has been carrying Palestinians' stories to the world throughout Israel's war.

The film is set in the period when Israel ordered Gaza City to be emptied. Hundreds of thousands of people were told to leave their homes, their neighbourhoods and whatever was left, and move south. Maram is reporting on this displacement, and at the same time she faces the very decision she asks others about: to go or to stay.

According to the film's introduction, three burdens travel with Maram in her daily life: a severe shortage of food, the responsibility of being a mother, and grief for fellow journalists killed in this war. The Gaza war is counted among the deadliest conflicts for journalists in recent history, and Al Jazeera itself has lost several of its reporters and camera operators.

Moving through the emptying city, Maram meets two kinds of people. Some have decided to leave, because staying feels like inviting death. Others have decided not to go, because for them leaving means losing home for ever, and nowhere in the south is truly safe either. The film listens to both choices with equal respect.

The film's weight lies in the fact that no distance is left between reporter and displaced. The journalist who asks a family in the morning where they will go is solving the same question for her own children in the evening. Reporting the news and being part of it go on side by side.

The film was made by Mohammed Sawwaf, Salah Al-Haw and Ibrahim Al-Otla, who have themselves been working in Gaza. Outside journalists were not allowed to enter Gaza freely, so the world has seen much of this war through the eyes of such local journalists.
nazar: In India the debate on Gaza often gets tangled in diplomacy and slogans for and against. This film reminds us that displacement is not a line drawn on a map but a matter of kitchens, children and neighbours.

It is also the story of journalists who report standing on the rubble of their own homes. From Kashmir to Manipur, where local journalists are often the only eyes, the question of their safety and freedom matters just as much to us.
sawal: When a reporter is emptying her own home, whose displacement does she record?
ref: Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary series in which filmmakers from around the world make short films about ordinary people's lives.
Forced displacement
Forcing people to leave their homes because of war or government orders. Under international humanitarian law, such displacement of civilians can be a serious violation.

h: When a writer's words start testifying against him
dek: Dinesh Shrinet asks whether a writer's life can be kept apart from the work, and says a reader's trust does not come that cheap.
body: In his column 'Unframed' on Hindwi's 'Bela', Dinesh Shrinet reopens an old debate: a writer is human too, so forgive his failings and read the work on its own. The mind accepts this argument, but the cheated reader does not. The piece looks for the reason behind that refusal.

Shrinet accepts that work and life do not run along one line. When a soldier who has lived through war writes an anti-war book, his hatred carries weight; a woman who cannot walk may watch children at play most closely. He gives the examples of Majid Majidi's 'Children of Heaven', the unfulfilled loves of Raj Kapoor and Yash Chopra, and Valmiki and Tulsidas. A lack often takes another shape in art. Still, he says, every word passes through the writer's values, and Vijay in Guru Dutt's 'Pyaasa' is a great poet precisely because he does not compromise his principles.

The heaviest part of the piece is personal. The writer says Nagarjun's poems were very dear to him, but after allegations of sexual abuse of a young girl came out after the poet's death, those poems began to feel hollow. It also hurts him that some poets and critics on social media began to question the survivor herself.

Shrinet links this debate to recent controversies: the questions raised about Alokdhanwa, and Amita Shireen's article on a biography of Firaq Gorakhpuri. He recalls Jack Zipes's reading of the folk tale 'Little Red Riding Hood', in which the wolf dressed as the grandmother is a metaphor for the hidden danger to young girls.

His conclusion is clear: the reader does not want a character certificate from the writer, but the assurance that he stands behind his words. One who cannot carry even that much accountability sees the weight of his work shrink too.
nazar: In the Hindi literary world, 'big names' are often protected at the cost of weaker voices. This piece challenges that habit head on and gives back to the reader the right not to hide their disillusionment.
In our view, allegations should remain allegations, but shying away from discussing them and putting the complainant in the dock are both equally unjust.
sawal: Was Vijay of 'Pyaasa' more honest than today's poets?
ref: Jack Zipes
American folklore scholar. In a 1993 book he read 'Little Red Riding Hood' as a warning to girls about sexual danger.
Unframed
Dinesh Shrinet's column on Hindwi's blog 'Bela', about the links between cinema, literature and society.
photo_note: A face lost in thought, Rabindranath Tagore

h: From a one-metre room to the banks of the Saryu, an account of grief
dek: Govind Nishad's memoir is about labour in a Delhi basti, homes ruined by drink, and the fear of turning to stone amid one death after another.
body: Govind Nishad's 'Pattharadil' (Heart of Stone), published on Hindwi's 'Bela', is a piece of autobiographical prose. It opens in Delhi's Choona Bhatti basti (settlement), where the writer looks for work all day in Shahdara, Naraina and Rajouri Garden, and at night sleeps on his brother's narrow balcony instead of in a stifling room one metre wide. He cannot get ahead in the long queue at the tubewell, and the city's language and manners feel foreign to him. The view of Delhi from a fourth floor in Kirti Nagar is his only freedom.

Then the story returns to the village, and a series of deaths begins. The brother with the balcony suffers liver failure; the family slowly goes numb with waiting, and the body is taken by boat to the Saryu. Machhli Bhaiya, who always asked after everyone, also dies of the same illness after a stay in an Azamgarh hospital. Sundar Bhaiya, who had an MA, sinks into drink and does not survive despite treatment in Chandigarh and Lucknow.

The writer is then studying history at Allahabad University, in a room in Holland Hall. News comes of the deaths of a nephew and two nieces; one niece dies soon after her wedding following a quarrel with her in-laws, and the in-laws take her body away. His family stops him from coming home out of fear of the police. Alone, he weeps, and turns to drink himself.

The central question of the piece is whether tears drying up means turning to stone. The writer says he did not want to die; he only wanted release from grief, guilt and fear. He leaves behind a list of questions about poverty, illness, alcohol and social fear.
At the end he writes that being unable to cry is not the absence of grief, and that the people he lost will live on in his words.
nazar: This memoir is a record of the India that gets entered in statistics as 'migrant workers' and 'liver disease'. Cheap liquor, broken healthcare and young men wandering in search of work: it all happens within one family.
In our view, the strength of such personal writing is that it turns the grief of homes on the margins into a question about the system.
sawal: Why did so many in one family die of drink and illness?
ref: Choona Bhatti
A crowded settlement in Delhi where many workers from outside live in small rented rooms.
Saryu
A river in Uttar Pradesh, another name for the Ghaghara. In the villages of Purvanchal, cremations take place on its banks.
photo_note: Ghat on a riverbank, Edwin Lord Weeks

h: Poems that insist on living with less in an age of markets
dek: Payal Bhardwaj reads Anupam Singh's second collection, 'Saanwali Ibaraten', as poetry that reaches beyond the female body to nature, riots and Palestine.
body: In Sammukh, Payal Bhardwaj reviews poet Anupam Singh's second collection, 'Saanwali Ibaraten' (Dusky Inscriptions). Published by Rajkamal Prakashan this year, it has eighty poems. The reviewer's opening point is that the book has come at a time when the market decides what we need, and the person who uses things is turning into a hoarder of them.

According to Bhardwaj, the first collection, 'Maine Gadha Hai Apna Purush' (I Have Shaped My Own Man), centred on a woman's body, desire and sense of self. This time the same awareness spreads outward: to nature, society, political violence and the crises of the world. The thread is one: keeping life going with simplicity and humanity. Opposition to consumerism and imperialism, the wish for a small home close to nature, and a view linked to environmental, feminist and Adivasi (indigenous) thought come up again and again in the review.

She pauses on some poems: one built on the metaphor of a window and a door, in which a woman sees the world only through the window; one in which the poet wishes to be a sanitation worker or a nurse; the pain of leaving home after marriage; and poems wrestling with patriarchy's hold over the body.

An important part of the review is the poems that record politics against Muslims, bulldozers and the fear of riots, and which, Bhardwaj says, do not turn into sloganeering. A poem written for Palestinian poets finds hope in children at play, and the Shillong poem questions the 'mainland' attitude towards the Northeast.

At the end she also notes a shortcoming: across eighty poems the themes repeat, and a stricter selection would have made the book stronger. Even so, she sees it as a successful effort to save justice, beauty and tenderness in harsh times.
nazar: New women's poetry in Hindi no longer speaks only of the body and the home; it takes in bulldozers, riots and Palestine too. This review shows how thin the wall between the personal and the political is.
The reviewer's honesty about the collection's weakness is also worth noting; it is rarely seen in Hindi reviewing.
sawal: Why does the poet want to be a sanitation worker or a nurse?
ref: Anupam Singh
Hindi poet. First collection 'Maine Gadha Hai Apna Purush', second 'Saanwali Ibaraten' (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2026).
photo_note: Villagers going to market, Amrita Sher-Gil

h: A whole empire on Calvino's chessboard, and an empty square at its heart
dek: In the sixteenth instalment of Sammukh's translation of 'Invisible Cities', Kublai Khan looks for the secret of his empire on a chessboard.
body: In Sammukh, young fiction writer Suman Shekhar is translating Italian writer Italo Calvino's book 'Invisible Cities' into Hindi in instalments. This is the sixteenth instalment of 'Adrishya Shahar' (Invisible Cities), and an editorial introduction has been published with it.

The introduction says the cities we live in slowly settle inside us: lanes, old houses, tea shops, smells and the small happenings of each day. When we leave a city, a piece of it comes along. The example is Allahabad, where someone who has left remembers the old church, Holland Hall, the ghats and the arguments at sweet shops. The introduction places Walter Benjamin's Berlin, Orhan Pamuk's Istanbul, Ahmed Ali's 'Twilight in Delhi', Sebald's 'Austerlitz' and Nirmal Verma in this same tradition of the remembered city.

In the translated passage, Marco Polo lays out things brought back from his travels, such as a helmet, a seashell, a coconut and a fan, on the coloured tiles beneath the emperor's throne. Kublai, a keen chess player, thinks that if cities also ran by the rules of chess, the whole empire could be understood without seeing every city. Marco turns the pieces into cities: the knight becomes a procession, the queen a woman standing on a balcony.

After the last journey, Kublai stops sending Marco out and the two simply go on playing. The emperor asks what winning and losing mean, and finally understands that every treasure of the empire is a shell, beneath which there remains a plain, empty square of wood.
This instalment gives the translation series a philosophical turn: power wants to know everything through maps and rules, but cities slip out of its grasp.
nazar: At a time when the names of cities are being changed and old settlements are being cleared by bulldozers, this passage reminds us that a city is not just an official map but a life that lives in people's memory.
Patient, instalment-by-instalment translation of world literature into Hindi is itself important work.
sawal: Can any emperor understand his empire through chess?
ref: Italo Calvino
Italian writer (1923-1985). In 'Invisible Cities' (1972), Marco Polo describes imaginary cities to Kublai Khan.
Kublai Khan
Thirteenth-century Mongol ruler and founder of China's Yuan dynasty, famous for the story of Marco Polo's arrival at his court.

h: Why name Bahraich when someone asks where Shravasti is?
dek: The first Hindi poems of Meerut's young poet Ravi speak of numbed citizens, questions of equality and a district missing from the news.
body: Sammukh has published six poems by Ravi, a young poet who teaches in Meerut. According to the introduction, he has so far written in English and appeared in a few magazines; this is his first publication in Hindi. We are not reproducing lines from the poems here, only giving a taste of them; the full poems can be read on Sammukh.

The first poem, 'Zombie', is about a citizen who, in boredom and self-blame, has grown content with his condition. Amid images of rotis baked on the coals of a funeral pyre, skeletons carried on shoulders and thirsty people drinking dirty water from potholes, a mocking voice declares the country dead, and the poem warns: do not become a zombie.

'Trishna ka Karan Kya?' (What Is the Cause of Craving?) asks questions in the manner of the Buddha, looks for the roots of longing in insecurity, want and humiliation, and asks whether inequality comes from birth or from deeds. 'Ekjut Rehna' (Staying United) argues that fear and oppression bind people together more than religion, caste or language. In 'Bhasha Ek Nadi Hai' (Language Is a River), grammar is the government and the government is a dam on the river, which breaks in the people's flood.

The most concrete poem is the last, 'Ghar Kahan Hai Aapka?' (Where Is Your Home?). The poet gives Bahraich to identify himself, but his real home is the nearby district of Shravasti: historic, but with no railway, a single bus to Delhi, an airport without flights, villages without electricity, fertile land that floods every year, contractors and middlemen, and workers migrating away.
The poet says the region is unknown because neither crime headlines, nor stars, nor toppers come from there. Farmers like Premchand's Hori are still there.
nazar: A poem like 'Ghar Kahan Hai Aapka?' maps the India that lies outside both claims of development and TV headlines. Shravasti is counted among the most backward districts in the country, and the poem records it not as a statistic but as lived experience.
That a poet writing in Hindi for the first time is so politically alert gives hope.
sawal: What does an airport without flights give Shravasti?
ref: Shravasti
A district in Uttar Pradesh and an ancient city linked with the Buddha. It is on NITI Aayog's list of aspirational districts, a region struggling with floods and migration.

h: The old poems of the novelist of 'Kala Pahad' return
dek: Janakipul carries five poems by Bhagwandas Morwal, holding memories such as tiled roofs, the smell of the Aravallis and a dry neem leaf.
body: On Janakipul, Prabhat Ranjan presents five poems by novelist Bhagwandas Morwal. In his introduction he recalls that in his school days, around 1985, he first read Morwal as a poet in 'Pravesh', the young poets' column of 'Kadambini'. Later they met in Delhi, by which time Morwal had come to be known as the novelist of 'Kala Pahad' (Black Mountain). His poetry collection 'Ghar ki Kisi Deewar Par' (On Some Wall of the House) has recently come out from Vani Prakashan. We are not reproducing lines from the poems here; the full text is on Janakipul.

In Morwal's own words, the bitter experiences of life's crooked paths and small, warm feelings pushed him towards poetry. 'Umr' (Age) speaks of borders, soldiers caught in barbed wire, and wounded, crippled bodies. 'Paiband' (Patch) is a poem of a past swept away in the city's flood and of the ancestors' voice that ears have grown too dull to hear.

'Ateet' (The Past) is like an exchange of letters and photographs, in which tiled roofs have turned into buildings glittering with electric light and shared memories have gone with them. 'Sansmaran' (Memoir) remembers an elder, 'Daddu', on a date in 1991: the smell of the Aravallis, tesu (flame of the forest) flowers, a tree felled in a storm that looks like an old man lying on a cot, and a photograph hanging on the wall after his death.
The last poem, 'Neem ki Patti-sa' (Like a Neem Leaf), is about a friendship gone numb: a dry neem leaf pressed in a history book and a smile frozen in a faded passport photo.
These poems give a glimpse of the early mind of a major prose writer, where the village of Mewat and the Aravallis survives as a memory from before the city's dazzle.
nazar: Morwal's novels are known for the lives of Mewat's Muslims and of people on the margins. In these poems the same village returns as tiled roofs, tesu and neem, a village that is fast vanishing in the race for development.
Rereading a writer's early poems also shows where the sensitivity of his prose came from.
sawal: When the tiled roof went, where did the shared memories go?
ref: Bhagwandas Morwal
Hindi novelist known for novels such as 'Kala Pahad', 'Babal Tera Des Mein' and 'Ret', set in the Mewat region.
Kadambini
A well-known Hindi monthly magazine of the Hindustan Times group, published from 1960 to 2020.
